name: Tesla

summary.text: Tesla, Inc. (Tesla Motors until 2017) is an electric-vehicle and energy-storage maker founded by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning. Secondary accounts say Elon Musk supplied most of its $7.5 million Series A round in February 2004 and became chairman and largest shareholder. It went public on Nasdaq on June 29, 2010 at $17 a share, raising about $226 million. The U.S. Department of Energy's Advanced Technology Vehicles Manufacturing program made $465 million in loan facilities available to it from January 2010; Tesla repaid the loan in full on May 22, 2013. Its annual reports show automotive regulatory credits revenue of $1.58 billion (2020), $1.47 billion (2021), $1.78 billion (2022), $1.79 billion (2023), $2.76 billion (2024) and $1.99 billion (2025).

History of Tesla, Inc.

facts.claim: Tesla was founded by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning; Elon Musk was not an original founder. Secondary accounts say Tesla raised about $7.5 million in a Series A round in February 2004, including about $6.5 million (some accounts say $6.35 million) from Musk, drawn from his PayPal proceeds, after which he became chairman of the board and the largest shareholder.
facts.quote: Including $6.5 million from Musk, who had received $176 million from the sale of his PayPal interest two years earlier.

facts.quote: the offering raised $226.1 million after selling 13.3 million shares for $17 apiece

facts.claim: Under the Department of Energy's Advanced Technology Vehicles Manufacturing (ATVM) loan program, the Federal Financing Bank made two multi-draw term loan facilities totaling $465.0 million available to Tesla beginning January 20, 2010, to fund the planned Model S factory and an electric powertrain facility; the loan had been announced in June 2009. Contemporary reports said $365 million was earmarked for the Model S factory and $100 million for the battery-pack and drivetrain facility.
facts.quote: The Federal Financing Bank made two multi-draw term loan facilities totaling $465.0 million available beginning on January 20, 2010.

facts.claim: On May 22, 2013 Tesla paid $451.8 million to retire the DOE loan facility nine years ahead of schedule: $441.0 million of outstanding principal and interest plus a $10.8 million early-repayment penalty, according to its fiscal 2014 annual report. The Department of Energy said Tesla elected to repay the entire remaining balance early, and CNBC reported it was the first automaker to repay an ATVM loan.
facts.quote: paid $451.8 million to settle all outstanding loan amounts of $441.0 million, including principal and interest, as well as an early repayment penalty of $10.8 million

facts.claim: Tesla's income statement in its fiscal 2022 annual report lists automotive regulatory credits revenue of $1,776 million for 2022, $1,465 million for 2021 and $1,580 million for 2020; the company says sales of these credits are recognized within automotive regulatory credits revenue in its consolidated financial statements.
facts.quote: Sales of these credits are recognized within automotive regulatory credits revenue in our consolidated financial statements.

facts.claim: Tesla's annual reports show automotive regulatory credits revenue of $1,790 million in 2023, $2,763 million in 2024 and $1,993 million in 2025. The fiscal 2024 report says the line rose $973 million, or 54%, from 2023, citing stronger demand for credits in North America as other automakers scaled back battery-electric plans; the fiscal 2025 report says it fell $770 million, or 28%, from 2024, and cites governmental and regulatory actions, such as the OBBBA, restricting certain credit programs.
facts.quote: Automotive regulatory credits revenue increased $973 million, or 54%, in the year ended December 31, 2024 as compared to the year ended December 31, 2023.

openQuestions: The 2004 Series A figures ($7.5 million round; $6.5 million or $6.35 million from Musk) come from Wikipedia, Yahoo Finance and CNN's timeline, not from Tesla's S-1 or a contemporaneous filing. The S-1's 'Certain Relationships' and beneficial-ownership sections should be checked.

Which regulatory programs the credits come from (California ZEV, federal GHG/CAFE, EU CO2 pooling) and that buyers are other regulated automakers: the 10-K passage describing this was not retrieved before the search budget ran out, so the brief's phrase 'ZEV credits paid by legacy automakers' is recorded only as 'automotive regulatory credits revenue' here. The fiscal 2024 10-K's attribution to 'other automakers' scaling back BEV plans was returned in paraphrase only.

Tesla's fiscal 2021 10-K narrative (credits of $1.46 billion, $1.58 billion and $594 million for 2021, 2020 and 2019) was returned in a search summary but the filing page itself was not in the results; the 2019 figure is therefore not recorded.
The DOE's own 2010 loan-closing release and the June 2009 award release were not retrieved; the January 20, 2010 date is from Tesla's S-1/A.
The 2004 Series A figures ($7.5M round, ~$6.5M from Musk) rest on secondary accounts; the Tesla S-1 passage on the 2004 round should be cited directly.
